text: There is an evil I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy upon humankind:

versions.text: There is an evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily on humanity:
versions.explanation: The Hebrew רַבָּה הִיא עַל means "it is abundant/common among" or "heavy upon" people. "Weighs heavily" is defensible, but "lies heavy upon humankind" reads slightly better aloud and avoids the redundancy of "heavily." Consider also a footnote noting the alternative sense "it is widespread among people."

text: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his soul desires—yet God does not let him enjoy it, and a stranger consumes it instead. This is meaningless, a grievous affliction.

A man may father a hundred children and live many years; yet however long his days may be, if his soul is not satisfied with good and he receives no burial, then I say the stillborn child is better off than he.

versions.text: A man may father a hundred children and live many years; yet however long his days may be, if he cannot savor the good and receives no proper burial, then I say the stillborn child is better off than he.
versions.explanation: "Cannot savor" softens the Hebrew לֹא־תִשְׂבַּע ("is not satisfied/filled"), and "proper" is added to קְבוּרָה, which simply means "burial." Keeping "satisfied" and plain "burial" is more accurate.

text: For it comes in emptiness and departs in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered over.

versions.text: For it arrives in vain and departs in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered over.
versions.explanation: The chapter renders הֶבֶל as "meaningless"/"empty" elsewhere (vv. 2, 9, 11). "Arrives in vain" shifts the sense toward futile effort rather than the emptiness/breath-like nothingness of the stillborn's coming, and "comes ... departs" preserves the Hebrew's parallel pairing more naturally for reading aloud.

text: It never saw the sun, never knew a thing—yet it has more rest than he does.

versions.text: It never saw the sun, never knew a thing—yet it has more rest than that man.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew is simply "this one has more rest than that one." "That man" makes explicit an identification that the text leaves open; "he does" is smoother for oral reading and still clear from context.

text: Even if he lived a thousand years twice over but never enjoyed the good—do not all go to the same place?
All a person's toil is for his mouth, and still the appetite is never filled.

versions.text: All a person's toil is for the mouth, and still the appetite is never satisfied.
versions.explanation: לְפִיהוּ has the possessive suffix ("his mouth"), which the current rendering drops; and תִמָּלֵא is "filled," which also avoids repeating "satisfied" from v. 3 and better matches the image of filling the mouth/appetite.

text: What advantage, then, has the wise over the fool? What does the poor man gain by knowing how to conduct himself before the living?
Better what the eyes can see than the wandering of desire. This too is meaningless, a chasing after wind.
Whatever has come to be was named long ago, and it is known that he is only a man: he cannot contend with one stronger than himself.

versions.text: Whatever exists has already been named, and what man is has long been known: he cannot contend with one stronger than himself.
versions.explanation: The clause וְנוֹדָע אֲשֶׁר־הוּא אָדָם means "and it is known that he is (merely) man" — a statement about human limitation that grounds the following clause. "What man is has long been known" shifts the sense and loses the logical link to the inability to contend with the stronger one. Also מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה is past ('whatever has been'), not present 'exists.'

text: For there are many words, and they multiply emptiness—so what advantage is there for anyone?

versions.text: The more words, the more meaningless it all becomes—and what does that profit anyone?
versions.explanation: The current rendering turns the Hebrew statement ("there are many words that increase emptiness") into a proverbial comparative construction and adds "does that profit," which misreads מַה־יֹּתֵר לָאָדָם ("what advantage has a person?"). Note also that דְּבָרִים can mean "things" as well as "words"; a footnote could mention this.

versions.text: For there are many words, and they only multiply what is empty—so what advantage is there for anyone?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew מַרְבִּים הָבֶל is a plain statement ("increasing emptiness"); "only" adds an emphasis not present in the source, and "what is empty" is a heavier phrase than the single noun הֶבֶל. "Multiply emptiness" is tighter and reads more smoothly aloud while keeping the chapter's consistent rendering of הֶבֶל.

text: For who knows what is good for a person in life, through the numbered days of his fleeting life, which he spends like a shadow? And who can tell anyone what will come after him under the sun?

versions.text: For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the few days of a fleeting life he passes like a shadow? Who can tell anyone what will come after him under the sun?
versions.explanation: מִסְפַּר יְמֵי is "the number of the days" (numbered days) rather than "few days," and the connective אֲשֶׁר at the start of the second question is dropped, leaving two abrupt questions; restoring "And" aids the oral flow.
